<reason>Both sides were disciplined, quotable, and format-compliant (clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structures; no fake sourcing). B built the more resilient architecture: the "credential as door, supervision as lock" design absorbed CON's safety case, the recognized-issuer-list answer defused the flood scenario with the devastating comparative jab that no registry exists to delist a lying landlord, and B converted A's own defense of residency-as-rationing into "rationing by wealth," which A never squarely escaped. A's strongest late point — supervision capacity drowning under a fast lane — was real but partially answered by B's mandatory-lock and funding responses, and A leaned heavily on a definitional move (any supervised bridging counts as residency) that B effectively exposed as making the motion unfalsifiable: "a dictionary, not a policy." A also had the last word in every chronological pairing and still left B's identical-safety/different-price weighing standing. B made the debate easier to decide: hypothetical floods versus today's actual short-staffed wards.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 A1/A2: recognized-issuer lists plus instant mass revocation answered the flood question at scale, the "no registry to delist a lying landlord" reversal won the verification clash, and showing the lock is a legal condition of practice (not a rival lane) neutralized A's starvation pressure while pinning A's case down to unfalsifiable relabeling.</best_rebuttal>
